- **TomasBM** (id 47055071, time 1771371627)
  - Hate to be the <i>party pooper</i>, but these two points are hardly evidence of an autonomous attack.<p>Don&#x27;t get me wrong: it would certainly be very valuable to any LLM developer or deployer to know that other plausible scenarios [1] have been disproved. Since LLMs are a black box, investigating or reproducing this would be very difficult, but worth the effort if there&#x27;s no other explanation. However, if this was not <i>caused</i> by the internal mechanisms of the model, it just becomes a fishing expedition for red herrings.<p>Things that would indicate no human intervention at any point in the chain:<p>- log of actual changes (e.g., commits) to configurations (e.g., system prompt, user prompts), before and after the event, not self-reported by the agent;<p>- log of the chat session inputs and outputs, and the agent thinking chain;<p>- log of account logins;<p>- info on the model deployment, OpenClaw configs, etc.<p>That said, this seems to be an example where many, including the author, want to discuss a particular cause (<i>instrumental convergence</i>) and its implications, regardless of the real cause. And that&#x27;s OK, I guess - maybe it was never about the <i>whodunnit</i>, but about the <i>what if the LLM agent dunnit</i>.<p>[1] I&#x27;ve discussed them in the thread of the first article, but shortly: human hiding actions behind agent; direct prompt (incl. jailbreak); system prompt (incl. jailbreak); malicious model chosen on purpose; fine-tuned jailbroken model.
